title: Nuevo Laredo Border Commerce Squeezed as U.S. Keeps Tamaulipas at Level 4 “Do Not Travel”
excerpt: With Tamaulipas reaffirmed at the U.S. Level 4 travel advisory, border businesses report closed shops, lost employers and medical and hotel visits down as much as 30%.
content:
Border commerce in Tamaulipas — including Nuevo Laredo — is operating under strain as the United States keeps the state at its highest travel warning, Level 4, with an explicit recommendation to its citizens not to travel because of the risk of violence, according to a November 3 report in Manifiesto Tamaulipas.

The report, citing the Federation of National Chambers of Commerce (Fecanaco), says the exodus of Texas shoppers, combined with rising violence, has left a trail of closed storefronts, lost jobs and capital flight of more than 100 million pesos a month across the state’s organized commerce sector. Reynosa, Matamoros and Nuevo Progreso face the deepest paralysis in cross-border consumption, their main economic engine, the report says.

Historically, the daily flow of U.S. citizens crossing to shop, dine or attend medical appointments sustained the local economy. Today, that engine is running at a minimum, the report says, as fear and road restrictions keep visitors away. Fecanaco president Abraham Rodríguez Padrón warned that U.S. travel alerts act as a psychological brake discouraging travel by U.S. citizens, hitting businesses that depend on Texas dollars to survive.

The official employer-registry figures cited in the report show the scale: Tamaulipas lost 1,766 registered employers in 2025, a 5.4 percent drop, more than double the national average of 2.4 percent, plus 779 more in the first half of 2026. Reynosa lost 336 employers in 2025 and 109 more between December and June 2026. Matamoros lost 329 employers in 2025, and Nuevo Laredo lost 61 during the first half of 2026.

In Reynosa, the report says, Texas visitors once injected an estimated 370 million pesos a month; local chamber president Gildardo López Hinojosa put monthly losses above 100 million pesos during the first half of 2026, with about 1,000 businesses closed in recent years and more than 4,000 direct commerce jobs destroyed. In the first quarter of 2026, 144 business robberies were reported in Reynosa — 43 percent of all commercial robberies in the state.

The pressure peaked on October 29, when a day of road blockades, traffic disruptions and temporary closures of international bridges paralyzed commercial and school activity in the city, the report says. The U.S. Consulate ordered its personnel to shelter in place, and on October 30 the U.S. government reaffirmed Tamaulipas at Level 4. Medical tourism and hotel stays in Reynosa and Nuevo Laredo are running at minimums, with arrivals of Rio Grande Valley patients and guests down as much as 30 percent, according to the report.

Why it matters for Laredo

Fecanaco cautions that violence is not the only cause of closures: tax pressures and commercial competition also weigh on business owners. But for Laredo, the stakes are direct: Nuevo Laredo’s shops, clinics and hotels are part of the same binational economy as Laredo’s bridges, warehouses and stores. When Texas shoppers stop crossing south, the loss is felt on both sides of the Rio Grande — and a Level 4 warning, by design, tells them not to go.

Sources:

  • Manifiesto Tamaulipas, “Comercio fronterizo sitiado por ‘Alerta 4’ de Washington” (Nov. 3, 2026)
